tasks.title: Famous mistranslations
tasks.html:
📚 Famous mistranslations

History is full of moments where a single word, badly rendered, changed everything. Diplomats have pointed out that one ambiguous verb in a 1945 reply was read as a cold rejection rather than a polite ‘no comment’. Translators later admitted the nuance had been impossible to carry across.

One airline claimed its slogan would ‘delight’ customers; in another market the literal translation promised something absurd, and rivals highlighted the blunder. The company apologised for the confusion and recommended rewriting its materials with local editors.

The lesson experts keep emphasising: translation is not word-swapping — it is carrying connotation, register and tone.

tasks.title: Why great applicants still get rejected
tasks.html:
📚 A recruiter’s honest advice

Let me be blunt: meeting the criteria is the bare minimum. In a competitive field, you must give us a reason to remember you. The candidates who get shortlisted are rarely the most qualified on paper — they’re the ones who tailored everything.

A few rules. You are required to follow the application instructions exactly. You don’t have to have every listed skill — show transferable skills and a willingness to learn. And you’d better research us properly: generic cover letters are bound to land at the bottom of the pile.

Rejection isn’t always about you. Sometimes an internal candidate was always likely to win. So you might want to keep applying and treat each ‘no’ as data, not a verdict.

When the floods hit, our street had been struggling for years — shops closing, neighbours barely speaking. Within hours, people who had never exchanged a word were rallying round, bailing out homes and sharing whatever they had.

Rarely do we admit how quickly we judge. Research suggests we form a first impression in well under a second; what we notice first is rarely what matters most. It was a friendly demeanour, one study found, that swayed people far more than actual competence.

📚 Why lies travel faster

Designed to provoke, false stories are built for sharing. Studies tracking millions of posts have found that misinformation, carrying more novelty and emotion, spreads faster than the truth. Posted at the right moment, a single dubious claim can reach millions before anyone thinks to fact-check it.

Having gone viral, a rumour becomes durable. Even when debunked, it lingers; people remember the claim long after forgetting the correction. Repeated often enough, hearsay starts to feel credible.

Researchers suggest that, offered early and from a trusted source, accurate information can slow the spread. Treated with healthy scepticism, even the most shareable claim loses some power.

tasks.title: Why a song gets stuck
tasks.html:
📚 The science of the earworm

Some tunes are merely quite catchy; others are absolutely impossible to shake. The stickiest songs share a fairly simple shape — a melody that rises and falls predictably, with one utterly unexpected leap to keep the brain hooked.

Lyrics matter too, though less than we think. A completely meaningless chorus can lodge in memory if the rhythm is right, while evocative words may slip away. The most haunting songs marry a childish hook to a slightly strange harmony.

So is the earworm a sign of brilliance? Not really. Some utterly timeless masterpieces never ‘stick’, while a fairly derivative jingle can haunt you for days. Catchiness is quite separate from quality.

tasks.title: Why more options make us miserable
tasks.html:
📚 The tyranny of choice

Ask people if they want more choice and most will say they do. But research suggests they shouldn’t. Faced with dozens of near-identical options, we don’t decide better — we dither, second-guess, and often don’t decide at all.
In one famous study, shoppers offered six jams bought happily; those offered twenty-four mostly didn’t. Too many options paralyse us. Even after we choose, more alternatives make us less satisfied: ‘I think it would,’ we tell ourselves — usually wrongly.
So what helps? Limit your options on purpose. Set criteria, weigh up the real pros and cons, and once you’ve made up your mind, stop. ‘Good enough’ beats ‘perfect’.

tasks.title: Are we really better connected?
tasks.html:
📚 The always-on life

In terms of convenience, the always-on life is hard to beat. We can work, shop and socialise without leaving the sofa. Yet on the whole, this connectivity comes at the expense of something harder to measure: our attention.
Studies point to a steady increase in screen time and a matching decline in deep focus. We’re aware of the problem — most admit to doomscrolling — but struggle to log off. The impact on sleep is well documented.
So what’s the answer? Not a total digital detox, but boundaries. With regard to wellbeing, small consistent limits beat dramatic ones. In the long run, the goal isn’t to go offline forever; it’s to decide, deliberately, when to.

📚 How records keep falling

For decades, the widely held belief that the four-minute mile was impossible went unchallenged. The barrier wasn’t in the legs; it was in the mind.
